row.basis: Moses before Pharaoh; refusal to heed
row.note: In the Bible’s Moses–Pharaoh scene, Pharaoh asks who YHWH is and says he will not obey YHWH’s voice or release Israel; this gives the commentary’s rejected summons to Pharaoh a concrete counterpart, while making Pharaoh’s claimed ignorance explicit.

row.basis: Pharaoh’s servants fear YHWH’s word
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears takes the reminder; during the hail warning, Pharaoh’s servants who feared YHWH’s word hurried their servants and livestock to shelter, showing fear as heedful response.

row.basis: Failure to set the heart on the warning
row.note: The next verse says those who did not set their heart on YHWH’s word left their servants and livestock in the field; it gives a precise refusal alongside the fear-led response in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Moses confronts Pharaoh’s refusal
row.note: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH and demand Israel’s release; this is the same ruler’s rejection of a divine summons, in the biblical narrative’s own terms.

row.basis: Hearing in order to learn fear
row.note: Moses recalls the assembly at Horeb so Israel would hear God’s words and learn to fear him throughout life, then teach their children; hearing instruction is explicitly the path to the reverent fear the commentary associates with receiving the reminder.

row.basis: Warning and reward in keeping instruction
row.note: The psalm says God’s rules warn the servant and that keeping them brings great reward; this joins an admonition’s warning function to a concrete benefit, as the commentary asks whether the reminder benefits.

row.basis: Wisdom calls and is refused
row.note: Personified Wisdom says she called and was refused and stretched out her hand without being heeded; this gives the bedbaht’s avoidance of offered admonition a specific scriptural scene.

row.basis: Different responses to rebuke
row.note: Proverbs says rebuking a scoffer brings hatred but rebuking a wise person brings love; like the commentary’s contrast between the one who takes the reminder and the one who avoids it, the response depends on the hearer.

row.basis: Instruction increases the wise hearer’s learning
row.note: The verse says instruction makes the wise wiser and teaching increases the righteous person’s learning; it supplies a concrete account of how admonition benefits the receptive hearer.

row.basis: Listening to life-giving reproof
row.note: The one whose ear listens to life-giving reproof dwells among the wise; this closely matches the commentary’s hearer who receives admonition through an inwardly responsive disposition.

row.basis: Ignoring instruction versus heeding reproof
row.note: Proverbs contrasts the person who ignores instruction and harms himself with the one who heeds reproof and gains understanding, spelling out both sides of the commentary’s reception/avoidance contrast.

row.basis: Fear, wisdom, and turning from evil
row.note: Job’s poem identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding; this brings together the commentary’s knowledge-inflected fear and the distance from wrongdoing suggested by its avoidance language.

row.basis: Trembling at God’s word
row.note: Isaiah says the Lord looks toward the lowly and contrite person who trembles at his word; this gives a scriptural profile for the commentary’s inwardly trembling hearer who receives admonition.

row.basis: A warning intended to turn its hearers
row.note: Jeremiah’s scroll is to recount coming disaster so Judah may hear, turn from evil, and be forgiven; the passage makes the intended benefit of a reminder explicit.

row.basis: Officials fear after hearing the scroll
row.note: After Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words, the officials look at one another in fear and say they must report them to the king; the warning produces the kind of fear-led attention that the commentary associates with receiving counsel.

row.basis: The king burns the warning
row.note: As the scroll is read, Jehoiakim cuts off its columns and burns them; the act gives a stark, material form to the commentary’s image of the wretched keeping the reminder at a distance.

row.basis: The king and his servants feel no fear
row.note: The verse says the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments after hearing the words; it contrasts their response with the officials’ fear in 36:16 and shows refusal despite access to the warning.

row.basis: Whether the rebellious hear or refuse
row.note: God tells Ezekiel that whether the rebellious house hears or refuses, its members will know a prophet has been among them; the message’s delivery is distinguished from its acceptance, as in the commentary’s divided audience.

row.basis: Speak the words whether heard or refused
row.note: Ezekiel is told to speak God’s words whether the rebellious hear or refuse; this clarifies the admonisher’s task even where the reminder may not benefit its audience.

row.basis: The warned wicked person who will not turn
row.note: The watchman is to warn the wicked; if the warned person does not turn, he dies in his iniquity while the watchman has delivered himself. This links offered warning, refusal, and consequence without making the messenger responsible for the hearer’s response.

row.basis: Hearing without doing
row.note: The people come to Ezekiel, sit before him, and hear his words, yet do not do them; their mouths show love while their hearts pursue gain. This complicates a simple hear/refuse split by showing outward attendance without inward reception.

row.basis: Turning away and stopping the ears
row.note: Zechariah says the ancestors refused to pay attention, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears; the bodily gestures make the commentary’s language of passing by an admonition concrete.

row.basis: A hardened heart that will not hear
row.note: The people made their hearts hard lest they hear the Torah and the words sent through earlier prophets, bringing great wrath; the verse ties refusal of warning to a chosen incapacity to receive it.

row.basis: Nineveh receives Jonah’s warning
row.note: After Jonah announces Nineveh’s overthrow, its people believe God, fast, and put on sackcloth; their response gives a narrative instance of warning being received and changing its hearers.

row.basis: God relents after seeing Nineveh’s response
row.note: The narrative says God saw that the Ninevites turned from their evil way and did not bring the announced disaster; this completes the warning’s benefit in the story with a changed outcome.

row.basis: Josiah hears the book and tears his clothes
row.note: When the king hears the words of the book of the law, he tears his clothes; the scene offers a concrete example of a hearer registering a warning rather than passing it by.

row.basis: A humbled response to heard words
row.note: Huldah says Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself when he heard the words against Jerusalem, so God heard him; this makes inward responsiveness and its consequence explicit.

row.basis: Despising words until judgment
row.note: The chronicler says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets until wrath came; it is a concentrated account of rejecting repeated admonition and its outcome.

row.basis: Those who fear speak to one another
row.note: Malachi describes those who fear YHWH speaking with one another while YHWH listens and records them; this turns the commentary’s fear-led reception into a communal exchange whose hearers are remembered by God.

row.basis: Hearing and doing the sayings of Jesus
row.note: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does them to a house built on rock; it gives a concrete outcome for receiving instruction rather than merely encountering it.

row.basis: Hearing without doing
row.note: Jesus contrasts the person who hears his words but does not do them with the wise builder; the foolish house’s collapse makes the consequence of non-reception concrete.

row.basis: Closed ears and an unhealed hearer
row.note: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah describes a people whose heart has grown dull and ears are hard, so they do not hear, understand, turn, and receive healing; it gives a scriptural account of refusal as blocked reception.

row.basis: Hearing, accepting, and bearing fruit
row.note: In the sower parable, good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this supplies a specific picture of a reminder that benefits its hearer.

row.basis: Refusal of Moses and the Prophets
row.note: In the rich man’s story, Abraham says that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead; the warning cannot be made effective by a more spectacular sign when prior admonition is refused.

row.basis: One proclamation, opposed receptions
row.note: Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing but God’s power to those being saved; one proclamation divides hearers by reception and outcome, like the commentary’s two responses.

row.basis: The message among those saved and perishing
row.note: Paul calls the apostolic mission Christ’s fragrance among both those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation reaches audiences whose outcomes differ, adding a Christian account of divided reception.

row.basis: A fragrance from death or from life
row.note: Paul specifies that the same fragrance is for one person from death to death and for another from life to life; this sharpens the commentary’s contrast between the person who receives the reminder and the one who avoids it.

row.basis: Daily exhortation against a hardened heart
row.note: Hebrews tells the community to exhort one another every day so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit; admonition is a mutual practice meant to keep hearers receptive.

row.basis: Hearing without hardening
row.note: Hebrews repeats, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”; this directly joins hearing a divine summons to the choice between receiving it and resisting it.

row.basis: The message that did not benefit its hearers
row.note: Hebrews says the good news heard by the wilderness generation did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this closely parallels the commentary’s question of whether the reminder benefits and makes faith the interpretive bridge.

row.basis: Doers rather than hearers only
row.note: James warns readers not to be hearers only who deceive themselves, but to do the word; this distinguishes exposure to instruction from receiving it in practice.

row.basis: The preacher’s duty to reprove and exhort
row.note: Timothy is charged to proclaim the word and to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with patience; this gives a concrete Christian formulation of the admonisher’s task even when response varies.

row.basis: A hearer who will not endure sound teaching
row.note: Paul says people will not endure sound teaching and will gather teachers to suit their desires; this describes avoidance as actively selecting away from admonition.

row.basis: Turning the ears from truth
row.note: Paul says they will turn their ears away from truth and toward myths; the bodily image of turning away closely specifies the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance.

row.basis: Mockery and postponement after Paul’s announcement
row.note: In Athens, some mock when Paul speaks of resurrection, while others say they will hear him again; the scene records distinct responses to a public religious summons.

row.basis: Some hearers join and believe
row.note: The following verse names people who join Paul and believe; it completes the same scene with the response of hearers who accept the proclamation.

row.basis: Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels the Arabic source root ذ ك ر and frames dhikrā as admonition; Hebrew זכר (zakar, “remember”) is cognate, and Moses uses it to command Israel to remember the wilderness road as a lesson in humility and keeping the commandments. The connection is the remembered lesson, not an equation of memory with admonition.

row.basis: Choosing life rather than death
row.note: Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life; this gives a specific choice-and-consequence frame alongside the commentary’s contrast between the wretched and the opposite of happiness.

row.basis: A blessed person refuses wicked counsel
row.note: The psalm calls blessed the person who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked; unlike the bedbaht who avoids divine admonition, this person’s distance is good because of what is refused, making the object of avoidance decisive.

row.basis: Fear as the beginning of wisdom
row.note: The psalm says fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom and that those who practice the commands have good understanding; it links fear and knowledge in the reverse direction from the commentary’s claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge.

row.basis: Eliphaz calls the reproved person happy
row.note: Eliphaz says the person whom God reproves is happy and should not despise divine discipline; this touches the commentary’s contrast between the bedbaht and happiness, while remaining Eliphaz’s counsel within Job’s debate rather than an unqualified narrator verdict.

row.basis: Rejected knowledge and unchosen fear
row.note: Wisdom’s opponents are said to hate knowledge and not choose fear of YHWH; alongside the commentary’s Arabic source note linking خشية to “I knew” and its claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge, Proverbs gives the relation in the opposite pedagogical direction.

row.basis: The listener’s security
row.note: Wisdom says whoever listens will dwell securely and be at ease without dread of disaster; this adds safety as the outcome of attending to counsel, while the commentary emphasizes the receiver’s fear as the disposition that makes listening possible.

row.basis: The word accomplishes its purpose
row.note: Isaiah compares God’s word to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth, saying the word accomplishes God’s purpose; beside the commentary’s “if the reminder benefits,” this presents divine speech as effective, though not necessarily beneficial to every hearer.

row.basis: Those who tremble at the word amid hostility
row.note: Isaiah addresses hearers who tremble at YHWH’s word and then describes brothers who hate and expel them; this places reverent reception amid social hostility, a sharper conflict than the commentary’s brief contrast of receiver and avoider.

row.basis: An offered way rejected by its hearers
row.note: Jeremiah urges people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not; the scene makes rejection of offered guidance explicit.

row.basis: A prophet heard as a pleasant song
row.note: Ezekiel says his hearers treat his words like a beautiful song and listen without doing them; the image adds a form of non-reception in which people enjoy the sound of admonition while its claim passes them by.

row.basis: Rejected knowledge and forgotten instruction
row.note: Hosea says the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because they rejected knowledge and forgot God’s teaching; it connects the commentary’s knowledge-and-fear discussion to the consequence of refusing instruction.

row.basis: Arabic dhikrā and Hebrew זכרון
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر as its source root and uses dhikrā for admonition; Malachi’s זכרון (zikaron, “remembrance”) uses the cognate Hebrew root for the record of those who fear YHWH and speak together, where the sense is memorial rather than instruction.

row.basis: Fearers reinterpreted as paired Torah learners
row.note: The Mishnah reads Malachi’s people who fear God and speak together as two who sit with words of Torah between them, with the divine presence among them; this rabbinic interpretation turns fearful reception into shared study, echoing the commentary’s description of admonition as passing to another.

row.basis: Fear as wisdom’s beginning
row.note: Ben Sira says fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; alongside the commentary’s account of fear as reverent and associated with knowledge, this Jewish wisdom text makes fear the entry into wisdom rather than its result.

row.basis: Listening yields knowledge
row.note: Ben Sira says the one who loves listening gains knowledge and the attentive person becomes wise; this gives a concise account of instruction benefiting a receptive hearer.

row.basis: Disciples blessed with seeing and hearing
row.note: Jesus tells his disciples their eyes and ears are blessed because they see and hear; this supplies the positive counterpart to the dull hearing in the preceding verse and to the commentary’s fear-led recipient.

row.basis: Joyful reception that does not last
row.note: In the sower parable, rocky-ground hearers receive the word at once with joy but fall away when trouble comes; this preserves a secondary case beyond simple acceptance or avoidance, where initial reception fails to endure.

row.basis: Failure to see as imposed blindness
row.note: Paul says the god of this age has blinded unbelievers’ minds so they cannot see the gospel’s light; this gives a different account of failed reception from the commentary’s active image of the wretched person avoiding the reminder.

row.basis: Doing the heard word brings blessing
row.note: James describes the person who looks into the law and perseveres as a doer who will be blessed in doing; it specifies the benefit of receiving instruction as practice, not mere hearing.

row.basis: God’s outstretched hands to a disobedient people
row.note: Paul quotes God’s all-day outstretched hands toward a disobedient and contrary people; the image pairs persistent invitation with refusal and gives a Christian rereading of Israel’s resistance to divine speech.

row.basis: Reproof as loving discipline
row.note: The risen Christ says he reproves and disciplines those he loves, then urges repentance; this Christian text interprets correction as care and gives the admonition a restorative purpose.

row.basis: Noah’s preaching and the hearers saved
row.note: Clement presents Noah as preaching repentance and says those who heeded were saved; this early Christian retelling makes the outcome of a received admonition explicit.

row.basis: The soils as different kinds of hearers
row.note: Chrysostom’s homily on the sower reads the soils as differing hearers of the word; this Christian interpretation develops why one proclamation bears fruit in some and not in others, much like the commentary’s two responses to reminder.

row.basis: Nocturnal emission and exclusion from camp
row.note: The commentary’s Arabic source note links junub with distance from prayer and the mosque; Deuteronomy orders a man with a nocturnal emission outside the camp until evening, a specific ritual-distance comparison, though its setting is the military camp and it says nothing about prayer.

row.basis: Washing and return at evening
row.note: Deuteronomy continues that the man washes and returns to camp at sunset; this clarifies the temporary boundary behind the commentary’s junub association while differing from its prayer-and-mosque framing.

row.basis: Hearing, fear, obedience, and well-being
row.note: After Israel hears God’s voice at Horeb, YHWH wishes they would keep a heart to fear him and his commands always, so it would go well with them and their children; this directly joins heard instruction, reverent fear, and benefit.

row.basis: The God-fearer is taught the way
row.note: The psalm asks who fears YHWH and answers that God will instruct that person in the way to choose; it reverses the commentary’s order in a useful way, making fear the disposition that receives instruction.

row.basis: Casting instruction behind oneself
row.note: In God’s indictment of people who recite his statutes, the wicked are said to hate discipline and cast God’s words behind them; this makes rejection of instruction a deliberate act, close to the bedbaht’s avoidance.

row.basis: Refusal followed by one’s own counsel
row.note: After Israel would not listen to God’s voice, the psalm says he gave them over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsel; this connects refusal of a divine reminder with self-directed wandering.

row.basis: The good outcome of listening
row.note: God says that if Israel would listen and walk in his ways, he would quickly subdue its enemies; the verse gives a concrete benefit that refusal has forfeited.

row.basis: The flock summoned to hear God’s voice
row.note: The psalm calls Israel the people of God’s pasture and the sheep of his hand, then says “today, if you hear his voice”; it frames reception of divine speech as the present duty of the addressed community.

row.basis: Do not harden the heart when hearing
row.note: The psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as at Meribah; it makes the inner refusal that counters a receptive, trembling hearer explicit.

row.basis: Fear expressed by hearing and serving
row.note: Samuel tells Israel that if they fear YHWH, serve him, and listen to his voice rather than rebel, they and their king will fare well; it directly links fear to taking divine instruction.

row.basis: Refusal brings the Lord’s hand against them
row.note: Samuel warns that if Israel will not listen to YHWH’s voice and rebels against his command, the Lord’s hand will be against them; this gives the non-hearing side its consequence.

row.basis: Obedience is better than sacrifice
row.note: Samuel tells Saul that listening to YHWH’s voice is better than sacrifice; the rebuke makes heedful response itself the required offering, not a religious substitute for it.

row.basis: Rejecting the word brings rejection
row.note: Samuel says Saul rejected YHWH’s word, so YHWH rejected him as king; this states the consequence of a ruler who hears the divine command but will not receive it.

row.basis: Instruction as a path of life
row.note: Proverbs says the one who heeds instruction is on a path of life, while the one who rejects reproof leads others astray; it gives both the benefit of receiving counsel and the danger of refusing it.

row.basis: The son who hears versus the scoffer
row.note: A wise son hears his father’s instruction, while a scoffer does not listen to rebuke; this is another precise contrast between a teachable recipient and one who avoids admonition.

row.basis: A stiff neck after repeated reproof
row.note: The person often reproved who stiffens his neck will suddenly be broken beyond healing; this develops the fate of persistent refusal beyond the single act of avoiding a reminder.

row.basis: Willing obedience and good outcome
row.note: Isaiah says that if the people are willing and obedient they will eat the good of the land; it specifies a benefit for taking the prophetic demand to heart.

row.basis: Refusal and rebellion bring destruction
row.note: The paired warning says that if the people refuse and rebel, they will be devoured by the sword; it makes refusal of the same summons a concrete opposite outcome.

row.basis: Hearing without understanding in Isaiah’s commission
row.note: Isaiah is told to tell the people to hear without understanding and see without perceiving; in its own setting this is a prophetic commission to an unreceptive audience, offering a stark counter-scene to the commentary’s hearer who takes admonition.

row.basis: A people unwilling to hear instruction
row.note: Isaiah calls them rebellious children who will not hear the instruction of YHWH; this directly names refusal of the teaching the commentary calls a reminder.

row.basis: Demanding smooth words from the prophets
row.note: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, but to prophesy smooth things; this gives a specific way of avoiding correction by trying to control what the admonisher may say.

row.basis: Asking the Holy One to leave
row.note: They demand that the prophet turn aside from the way and that Israel’s Holy One cease from before them; this sharpens the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance into rejection of its divine source.

row.basis: The God-fearer listens to the servant’s voice
row.note: Isaiah asks who fears YHWH and obeys the voice of his servant, then tells that person to trust in YHWH while walking in darkness; this joins fear and listening while adding trust in a difficult circumstance.

row.basis: The wicked are urged to turn and receive pardon
row.note: Isaiah tells the wicked to forsake their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon; this shows prophetic admonition offered for a hearer’s benefit, not only to announce judgment.

row.basis: Turn so wrongdoing will not become ruin
row.note: Ezekiel urges Israel to repent and turn from its transgressions lest iniquity become its downfall; this makes the warning’s practical benefit explicit.

row.basis: Turn and live rather than die
row.note: YHWH says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death and commands Israel to turn and live; this places a life-giving invitation beside the commentary’s contrast of the one who receives counsel and the wretched one who avoids it.

row.basis: God calls the wicked to turn from death
row.note: YHWH swears he takes no pleasure in the wicked person’s death but wants that person to turn and live, repeating “turn back”; it makes the offered warning’s life-preserving purpose unmistakable.

row.basis: Those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words
row.note: Ben Sira says those who fear the Lord will not disobey his words and those who love him keep his ways; this directly links reverent fear with receiving and following instruction.

row.basis: Jerusalem is unwilling to be gathered
row.note: Jesus says he often wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood, but they were unwilling; the image makes refusal of a protective summons concrete.

row.basis: The word held fast and made fruitful
row.note: Jesus says good-soil hearers hold the word fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience; this specifies an enduring form of the beneficial reception described in the commentary.

row.basis: Take care how you hear
row.note: Jesus warns his hearers to consider how they hear, since the one who has will receive more and the one who lacks will lose even what he thinks he has; this makes the consequences of response explicit.

row.basis: Blessing belongs to those who keep the word
row.note: Jesus says blessed are those who hear God’s word and keep it; this pairs reception with obedience and the blessed outcome that contrasts with the commentary’s unhappy avoider.

row.basis: Hearing and believing lead from death to life
row.note: Jesus says the one who hears his word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life; the verse links reception to a changed fate.

row.basis: Refusing to come for life
row.note: Jesus tells his interlocutors that they are unwilling to come to him to have life; this is a direct instance of refusing the offered source of life.

row.basis: Rejected words become the judge
row.note: Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge: the word he spoke will judge on the last day; it connects non-reception to the judgment that follows.

row.basis: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
row.note: Stephen accuses his hearers of always resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did; this gives rejection of divine speech a repeated communal history.

row.basis: Paul says his hearers thrust aside the word
row.note: Paul and Barnabas say their audience judged itself unworthy of eternal life by thrusting aside God’s word, so they turn to the Gentiles; this concretely depicts a hearer’s active rejection of the announcement.

row.basis: Gentile hearers rejoice and believe
row.note: The Gentiles rejoice when they hear Paul’s message and believe; this supplies the receptive counterpart in the same proclamation scene.

row.basis: Different responses to Paul’s explanation
row.note: After Paul explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the prophets, some are persuaded and others disbelieve; this is a clear scene of one teaching meeting divided responses.

row.basis: Pay closer attention lest hearers drift away
row.note: Hebrews urges readers to pay closer attention to what they heard so they do not drift away from it; this makes avoidance a gradual slipping from an already heard warning.

row.basis: Neglecting salvation has no escape
row.note: Hebrews asks how anyone can escape if they neglect such a great salvation; this adds the consequence of letting a saving announcement pass by.

row.basis: Do not refuse the one speaking
row.note: Hebrews warns its readers not to refuse the one speaking from heaven and recalls that those who refused the earthly warning did not escape; it explicitly joins refusal of admonition with judgment.

row.basis: Receive the implanted word that can save
row.note: James tells readers to put away wickedness and receive meekly the implanted word, which can save their souls; this makes admonition a saving gift that must be welcomed.

row.basis: Bringing a wanderer back from error
row.note: James says whoever brings a person wandering from truth back saves that person from death and covers many sins; this gives the reminder a neighbor-directed, restorative action.

row.basis: Knowing God and hearing his messengers
row.note: John says whoever knows God listens to the apostolic witnesses, while one not from God does not listen; this directly ties knowledge to receptivity, complementing the commentary’s discussion of knowledge and fear.

row.basis: Prophetic speech as judicial hardening
row.note: Isaiah’s commission continues by telling him to make the people’s heart dull and ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed; unlike the commentary’s account of the wretched person avoiding a reminder, this passage portrays non-reception within a judgment commission.

row.basis: Discipline understood as a father’s instruction
row.note: Moses tells Israel to know in its heart that YHWH disciplines it as a father disciplines a son; this offers a Jewish scriptural frame in which correction itself is instruction, though it does not describe the audience’s response to a spoken reminder.

row.basis: Sinai’s acceptance under threat and later reaffirmation
row.note: The Talmud imagines the mountain held over Israel as a barrel, with acceptance of Torah demanded under threat of burial, then says Israel reaffirmed acceptance in Ahasuerus’s days; this complicates a simple equation of reception with inward reverent fear by distinguishing coerced and later willing acceptance.

row.basis: Isaiah’s hard-hearing prophecy applied to Paul’s audience
row.note: Paul quotes Isaiah’s dull ears and closed eyes to explain why some hearers will not understand, turn, and be healed; this Christian continuation shows an interpretive tradition applying Isaiah’s account of failed reception to a new audience.

row.basis: Clement’s Jonah as a model of heeded warning
row.note: Clement recalls that Jonah preached destruction to Nineveh and that the city repented and obtained pardon; this early Christian retelling reads the scriptural warning as a summons whose reception changes the announced outcome.
